messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

When Thomas was twelve, his stepfather’s sudden, iron-clad grip around his torso during a heated argument pressed a sharp, freezing cold through his shirt against the linoleum floor. That exact temperature on his skin still arrives without warning decades later, instantly pulling his own heart into a frantic pound. Each time the phantom chill hits, a memory of the event coming to mind suddenly strips away his present reality, cementing his conviction that he was permanently an outsider. Thomas had come to believe that the world was fundamentally hostile, a conviction that first took root in that kitchen and now dictates how he moves through his days. What frightened him most was how his entrenched sense of alienation made a simple draft or a cold coffee mug feel like a direct prelude to danger. Working as a software engineer in a glass-walled open floor plan meant Thomas spent his days navigating a landscape that constantly fed his hyperarousal. When a server room fan kicked on and dropped the ambient temperature near his workstation, his body reacted to danger before he had even time to think. That physiological surge immediately pulled another sudden memory to the forefront of his mind, causing his physiological alarm to dictate the frequency of his intrusive recollections. He found himself constantly noticing potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, a habit that turned a routine office tour into a tactical exercise. The relentless mental tally of exits and heavy office furniture only made his nervous system hypersensitive to the next subtle temperature shift on his skin, ensuring that these sensory cues continuously amplified his sense of imminent threat. Believing people could not be trusted, Thomas gradually stopped attending team lunches and began declining invitations to social contacts he used to enjoy. His wife, a graphic designer who worked from home, had long noticed his growing withdrawal, yet she could not penetrate the wall of his preparedness. Every avoided conversation and every cancelled weekend outing only deepened his conviction that proximity to others invited unpredictability, cementing his mistrust as an absolute truth. His refusal to allow casual contact also meant his mind had no alternative narrative to counter his worst fears, so his belief that he had to be especially careful became a relentless engine for his constant vigilance. Paying attention to or looking at his own body in the mirror or checking his posture only heightened his awareness of a specific temperature on his skin, which in turn made his heart race before his mind could ground him. When his wife finally placed a hand on his arm during their anniversary dinner, the sudden physical contact startled him so violently he knocked his water glass over. That concrete breaking point forced him to finally schedule an intake session. He came seeking a way to quiet the constant vigilance that had turned his life into a perimeter defense, hoping instead to simply feel safe in his own skin again.
